```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4, eval = requireNamespace("bayesplot", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("loo", quietly = TRUE))
```

Gratia can prepare posterior predictive checks for bayesplot and observation
log likelihoods for loo. Both packages are optional: install them to use their
methods. `log_lik()` itself needs neither package. The existing `appraise()` and
`posterior_predictive_plot()` functions also work without them.

Some bayesplot plots, including `error_binned` and the LOO-PIT plots, also
require bayesplot's optional rstantools package; install it with
`install.packages("rstantools")` to use those plots.

```{r models}
library("mgcv")
library("gratia")
set.seed(278)
dat <- data.frame(x = runif(100, -1, 1))
dat$y <- rpois(nrow(dat), exp(.3 + sin(3 * dat$x)))
linear <- gam(y ~ x, data = dat, family = poisson(), method = "REML")
smooth <- gam(y ~ s(x, k = 7), data = dat, family = poisson(), method = "REML")
```

## Check replicated responses

For each coefficient draw, a posterior predictive check generates another
response at every fitting observation. The variation between these replicated
data sets includes coefficient uncertainty and response variation.

```{r predictive-checks}
bayesplot::pp_check(smooth, type = "dens_overlay", n_draws = 20, seed = 42)
bayesplot::pp_check(smooth, type = "stat", stat = "sd", n_draws = 500, seed = 42)
```

The first plot compares the observed response distribution with replicated
distributions. The second checks whether their standard deviations cover the
observed standard deviation. Other bayesplot statistics can be supplied through
`stat`, including a function such as `function(y) mean(y == 0)` for the proportion
of zeroes. To display predictions alone, use `prefix = "ppd"`.

Grouped plots accept a fitting-frame variable name or a vector in fitting-row
order. A vector is useful when the grouping variable was not used in the model.

```{r grouped-check}
bayesplot::pp_check(smooth, type = "stat_grouped", stat = "mean", n_draws = 500,
  group = factor(dat$x > 0, labels = c("negative x", "positive x")), seed = 42)
```

Missing fitting rows are omitted consistently from responses and covariates.
Binomial checks use success counts and fitted trial counts; gratia's own
posterior predictive plots use proportions. Multivariate and grouped-family
models require `response`, for example `"response1"` or `"component2"`. These
selections keep distinct responses and observation families from being pooled.
For gamm/gamm4 fits, `conditioning` retains its existing gratia meaning.

## Evaluate observed-response log likelihoods

`log_lik()` holds each response at its observed value and evaluates its log
density or log probability mass at each coefficient draw. Rows are posterior
draws and columns are retained fitting observations. For example, a Poisson
entry is `dpois(y[i], lambda = mu[s, i], log = TRUE)`.

```{r log-likelihood}
ll <- gratia::log_lik(smooth, n_draws = 2000, seed = 42)
dim(ll)
head(attr(ll, "observation"))
attr(ll, "gratia")
```

These values include the fitting likelihood's normalising constants and weights,
but exclude smoothing penalties. They differ from the single fitted log
likelihood returned by `stats::logLik(smooth)`, whose existing behaviour is
unchanged. A multivariate-normal observation contributes a joint density for
its complete response vector. Grouped-family rows use their respective family.

## Compare predictive performance with loo

Loo uses importance weights to approximate the predictions obtained by leaving
one observation out. Its `elpd_loo` estimate summarises expected log predictive
density: larger values indicate better predictions on the same response scale
and the same observations.

```{r loo-comparison}
loo_linear <- loo::loo(linear, n_draws = 2000, seed = 42)
loo_smooth <- loo::loo(smooth, n_draws = 2000, seed = 42)
loo::loo_compare(loo_linear, loo_smooth)
loo::pareto_k_table(loo_smooth)
```

The methods return ordinary loo objects, so loo's plotting, model-comparison
and weighting tools are available. For an already extracted matrix of
independent Gaussian coefficient draws, the equivalent calculation is
`loo::loo(ll, r_eff = 1)`. `loo::waic(smooth, n_draws = 2000, seed = 42)` also works.
Model methods evaluate likelihoods one observation at a time, avoiding a full
draws-by-observations matrix unless saved PSIS weights are requested.

Large Pareto-k values identify observations whose omission is difficult to
approximate by reweighting the existing draws. Inspect these observations and
loo's warnings before relying on a comparison. Use explicit refits or a separate
cross-validation analysis when reweighting is unreliable; these methods do not
automatically refit models or perform moment matching.

LOO predictive plots use response simulations and importance weights from the
same coefficient draws:

```{r loo-plot, eval=requireNamespace("bayesplot", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("loo", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("rstantools", quietly = TRUE)}
bayesplot::pp_check(smooth, type = "loo_pit_overlay", n_draws = 2000, seed = 42)
```

## Understand the posterior approximation

By default, gratia draws coefficients jointly from mgcv's Gaussian approximation.
For a distributional GAM, this includes coefficients for each distribution
parameter. For multivariate-normal likelihoods, it also includes the fitted
precision-matrix coefficients. Scale, shape and other parameters outside the
coefficient vector stay at fitted values, as do smoothing parameters.

This is a conditional approximation, rather than a procedure that re-estimates
every parameter for every omitted observation. `unconditional = TRUE` can use
mgcv's corrected coefficient covariance when available, but it does not draw
those other parameters jointly. PSIS calculations do not correct the Gaussian
approximation, and small Pareto-k values do not establish its accuracy.

```{r sampling-options, eval=FALSE}
# Extra sampler arguments are kept separate from loo and plotting arguments.
loo::loo(smooth, n_draws = 2000, seed = 42,
  sampling_args = list(unconditional = TRUE))
bayesplot::pp_check(smooth, n_draws = 50, seed = 42,
  sampling_args = list(unconditional = TRUE))

# Four chains share the total retained count, with separate burn-in.
loo::loo(smooth, n_draws = 2000, seed = 42,
  sampling_args = list(method = "mh", chains = 4, burnin = 1000))
```

For supplied coefficient draws, use `method = "user", draws = B` in
`log_lik()`, or place those arguments in `sampling_args` for loo and bayesplot.
LOO uses the chain and iteration mapping stored by gratia's samplers. For an
unlabelled matrix, supply `chain_id` or an explicit `r_eff`; gratia cannot infer
chain boundaries from its dimensions. A supplied `chain_id` must agree with
stored metadata. Bootstrap coefficient
samples do not become posterior draws by passing them to this interface.

`n_draws` is the total retained count, so 2,000 draws over four chains retains
500 draws per chain. Likelihood and LOO/WAIC wrappers default to 4,000 draws;
bayesplot uses 50 for ordinary checks and 4,000 for leave-one-out plots.
Supplied matrices determine their own count and chains. These wrappers reject
the obsolete `n` argument, and inactive sampler controls produce errors.
Use `diagnostics = TRUE` directly in `log_lik()`, or in `sampling_args` for LOO
and bayesplot, to retain coefficient diagnostics. The likelihood matrix also
supports `as_mcmc_draws()` for diagnostics of its observation-wise log densities.

Likelihood and LOO methods initially cover independent GAM/BAM responses. They
exclude residual-correlated BAMs, full gamm/gamm4 fits, quasi families, Cox
partial likelihoods and censored observation processes. Supported ordinary
posterior predictive checks retain their existing model coverage. With
random-effect smooths, observation-level LOO predicts further observations in
the fitted groups; it does not leave out entire groups.

The reproducible script `inst/validation/loo-refits.R` compares representative
Gaussian, Poisson and binomial PSIS results with explicit leave-one-out refits.
It distinguishes refits that hold smoothing and nuisance parameters fixed from
refits that re-estimate them.
